questions.q: One mole of any substance contains:
questions.solution:
**Avogadro's number**, $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles.

It is simply a counting unit, like 'a dozen' — chosen so that one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative formula mass.

questions.q: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the products is:
questions.solution:
**Equal** — atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.

An apparent loss usually means a gas has escaped; an apparent gain usually means a gas from the air has been taken in, as when magnesium burns.

**Exothermic** means heat is given out, so the surroundings warm up and $\Delta H$ is **negative**.

Combustion, respiration, neutralisation and most displacement reactions are exothermic.
options: heat is absorbed and the temperature falls
heat is released and the temperature rises

questions.q: In a chemical reaction, breaking bonds is:
questions.solution:
**Breaking** bonds always requires energy — it is **endothermic**. **Making** bonds releases it.

Whether the reaction overall gives out or takes in heat depends on which is larger: if more energy is released making new bonds than was spent breaking old ones, the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: The empirical formula of a compound shows:
questions.solution:
The **empirical** formula is the simplest ratio; the **molecular** formula is the actual count.

Glucose is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$ molecularly but $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$ empirically. Ionic compounds only ever have an empirical formula, since there are no molecules.
options: the actual number of atoms in a molecule
the simplest whole number ratio of atoms

questions.q: How many moles are there in $36$ g of water? ($M_{r}$ of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O} = 18$.)
Find the mass (in g) of $0.5$ mol of $\text{CaCO}_{3}$. ($M_{r} = 100$.)
Find the relative formula mass of $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. (H $= 1$, S $= 32$, O $= 16$.)
Find the percentage by mass of oxygen in water, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ ($M_{r} = 18$), correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{16}{18} \times 100 = \mathbf{88.9}\%$.

Water is nearly nine-tenths oxygen by mass, though two-thirds of its atoms are hydrogen — mass and number are quite different questions.

questions.q: What volume (in dm$^{3}$) does $1$ mol of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{24}$ dm$^{3}$ at RTP (and about $22.4$ dm$^{3}$ at s.t.p.).

The same for **every** gas, because the molecules are so far apart that their own size makes no difference — which is Avogadro's law.

questions.q: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed when $6$ g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen. ($\text{Mg} = 24$, $\text{O} = 16$.)
questions.solution:
**Equation:** $2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_{2} \to 2\text{MgO}$

**Moles of magnesium:**

$n = \dfrac{6}{24} = 0.25$ mol.

**Mole ratio.** From the equation, $2$ Mg give $2$ MgO — a $1:1$ ratio, so $0.25$ mol of MgO is formed.

**Mass of MgO.** $M_{r} = 24 + 16 = 40$:

$\text{mass} = 0.25 \times 40 = \mathbf{10}$ g.

**Check by conservation of mass.** The oxygen gained must be $10 - 6 = 4$ g, which is $\dfrac{4}{32} = 0.125$ mol of $\text{O}_{2}$.

And the equation says $2$ Mg need $1$ $\text{O}_{2}$, so $0.25$ mol of Mg needs $0.125$ mol ✓

**The three-step method** works for every such question: **mass $\to$ moles $\to$ (ratio) $\to$ moles $\to$ mass**. The balanced equation supplies the ratio and nothing else does.

questions.q: A compound contains $40\%$ carbon, $6.7\%$ hydrogen and $53.3\%$ oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula, and its molecular formula given that its relative molecular mass is $180$.
questions.solution:
**Take 100 g**, so the percentages become masses in grams.

**Divide each by its relative atomic mass to get moles:**

C: $\dfrac{40}{12} = 3.33$

H: $\dfrac{6.7}{1} = 6.7$

O: $\dfrac{53.3}{16} = 3.33$

**Divide through by the smallest** ($3.33$):

C: $1$, $\quad$ H: $2$, $\quad$ O: $1$

**Empirical formula: $\mathbf{\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}}$.**

**Molecular formula.** The empirical mass is $12 + 2 + 16 = 30$.

$\dfrac{180}{30} = 6$, so multiply every subscript by 6:

$\mathbf{\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}}$ — glucose.

**The method in one line:** percentage $\to$ moles $\to$ simplest ratio. And if the ratio comes out as something like $1 : 1.5$, multiply everything by 2 rather than rounding.

questions.q: Explain exothermic and endothermic reactions using energy level diagrams and bond energies, and calculate $\Delta H$ for a reaction in which $2500$ kJ is needed to break bonds and $2800$ kJ is released in making them.
questions.solution:
**Exothermic.** Heat is released, the surroundings warm, and $\Delta H$ is **negative**.

On an energy level diagram, the products are **below** the reactants; the difference is the energy given out.

**Examples:** combustion, respiration, neutralisation, most displacement reactions.

**Endothermic.** Heat is absorbed, the surroundings cool, and $\Delta H$ is **positive**.

The products are **above** the reactants.

**Examples:** thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.

**Both diagrams show an activation energy hump** — the energy needed to get started, even for an exothermic reaction. Petrol does not ignite on its own.

**Bond energies.**

• **Breaking** bonds is endothermic (energy in)

• **Making** bonds is exothermic (energy out)

$\Delta H = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$

**The calculation:**

$\Delta H = 2500 - 2800 = \mathbf{-300}$ kJ/mol.

**Negative, so the reaction is exothermic** — more energy came out forming the new bonds than went in breaking the old ones.

That is the whole basis of a fuel: the bonds in carbon dioxide and water are stronger than those in the hydrocarbon and oxygen, and the difference is what heats the house.

questions.q: Define concentration, and calculate the concentration in mol/dm$^{3}$ of a solution containing $4$ g of $\text{NaOH}$ in $250$ cm$^{3}$. ($M_{r}$ of $\text{NaOH} = 40$.)
questions.solution:
**Concentration** — the amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution.

$\text{concentration (mol/dm}^{3}) = \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume in dm}^{3}}$

**Moles of NaOH:**

$n = \dfrac{4}{40} = 0.1$ mol.

**Volume in dm$^{3}$.** $1$ dm$^{3} = 1000$ cm$^{3}$, so

$250$ cm$^{3} = 0.25$ dm$^{3}$.

**Concentration:**

$c = \dfrac{0.1}{0.25} = \mathbf{0.4}$ mol/dm$^{3}$.

**In g/dm$^{3}$:** $0.4 \times 40 = 16$ g/dm$^{3}$.

**The unit trap.** Volumes are measured in cm$^{3}$ in the laboratory and used in dm$^{3}$ in the formula. Converting **before** dividing — not after — is what keeps titration calculations honest.

questions.q: Balance $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + \text{O}_{2} \to \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and state the mole ratio of propane to oxygen.
questions.solution:
**Balance carbon first.** Three carbons on the left need $3\text{CO}_{2}$:

$\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + \text{O}_{2} \to 3\text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Then hydrogen.** Eight hydrogens need $4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$:

$\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + \text{O}_{2} \to 3\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Oxygen last**, since it appears in two products. The right side now has $3(2) + 4(1) = 10$ oxygen atoms, which is $5\text{O}_{2}$:

$\mathbf{\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + 5\text{O}_{2} \to 3\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}}$

**Check:** C $3 = 3$ ✓, H $8 = 8$ ✓, O $10 = 10$ ✓

**Mole ratio of propane to oxygen: $\mathbf{1 : 5}$.**

**The order matters.** Balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen — oxygen last because it is in several compounds, so leaving it until the end means only one number is left to adjust.

That $1:5$ ratio is why a gas burner needs a good air supply: burning propane takes five times its own volume of oxygen, and without it the flame goes yellow and sooty.
